rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Define barrier potential. Why does the thickness of the depletion layer in a p-n junction diode vary with increase in reverse bias ?
rows.solution:
**Barrier potential.**

The potential difference that develops **across the depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction**, opposing the further diffusion of majority carriers across it.

It is set up by the immobile ions left behind when diffusion strips the junction of mobile carriers — negative acceptor ions on the p-side, positive donor ions on the n-side — so the n-side sits at a higher potential than the p-side. Its size depends on the semiconductor: about \(0{\cdot}3\) V for germanium and \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon.

No battery is involved. The junction builds its own barrier and stops when the drift it drives exactly cancels the diffusion that created it.

**Why the depletion layer thickens as the reverse bias grows.**

In **reverse bias** the p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive. The applied field then points the **same way** as the junction's own field, so the two add:

\(V_{\text{total}} = V_B + V_{\text{applied}}\)

Two things follow, and they are the same thing seen from two sides.

*In terms of the carriers.* The external supply pulls majority carriers **away** from the junction — holes are drawn towards the negative terminal, electrons towards the positive. Both retreat from the junction, uncovering a further layer of immobile ions on each side. That newly uncovered layer is new depletion region, so the layer **widens**.

*In terms of charge.* A higher potential difference across the junction requires a larger separated charge to support it, and the only charge available is the fixed ionic charge. More ions must be uncovered, which means a thicker layer.

**The contrast with forward bias makes the mechanism clear.** There the applied voltage opposes \(V_B\), pushing majority carriers *towards* the junction, where they neutralise the ions. The layer **narrows**, the barrier falls, and once the applied voltage approaches \(V_B\) the junction conducts freely.

So the width of the depletion layer is not a fixed property of the diode but a **voltage-controlled** one — and that is exactly what a varactor diode exploits, since a wider layer means a smaller junction capacitance \(C \propto 1/W\).

rows.stem: Briefly explain how bright and dark fringes are formed on a screen due to the diffraction at a single slit. Hence, explain why the intensity at the bright fringes decreases sharply as their order (n) increases.
rows.solution:
**The starting point.** Every point of the wavefront in the slit acts as a secondary source, and the pattern at any point on the screen is the **sum of all those contributions with their proper phase differences**. Diffraction is therefore interference of a wave with itself, not of two separate beams. If the slit has width \(a\) and the light leaves at angle \(\theta\), the path difference between the two *edges* of the slit is

\(\mathrm{NP} - \mathrm{LP} = a\sin\theta \approx a\theta\)

**The central bright fringe.**

At the centre \(C\), \(\theta = 0\). Every path difference is zero, so **all** parts of the slit arrive in phase and reinforce. This gives the maximum possible intensity, and it is the only point where the whole slit contributes in step.

**The dark fringes.**

Take \(\theta = \lambda/a\), so the edge-to-edge path difference is exactly \(\lambda\). Now divide the slit into two halves. Every point in the upper half has a partner in the lower half exactly \(a/2\) away, whose path differs by \(\lambda/2\) — that is, **exactly out of phase**. The contributions cancel in pairs, and the whole slit gives nothing.

The same pairing works whenever the slit can be divided into an even number of such cancelling strips:

\(a\sin\theta = n\lambda, \qquad n = \pm1, \pm2, \pm3, \ldots\)

Note the peculiarity: for a *single slit*, \(a\sin\theta = n\lambda\) is the condition for **darkness**, the exact opposite of its meaning in a double slit.

**The secondary bright fringes, and why they are weak.**

Take \(\theta = 3\lambda/2a\), midway between the first two minima. Divide the slit into **three** equal parts. Across the first two-thirds the path difference is \(\lambda\), so by the argument above those two thirds cancel each other completely.

Only the **remaining one-third** of the slit contributes to the light at this point. It is bright — but it is built from a third of the slit rather than all of it, so it is far weaker than the centre.

This is the answer to the last part of the question. The secondary maxima lie at

\(a\sin\theta = \left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

and at each one the slit divides into \(2n+1\) parts of which \(2n\) cancel in pairs. So the fraction of the slit that survives is

\(\dfrac{1}{3}, \quad \dfrac{1}{5}, \quad \dfrac{1}{7}, \ \ldots\)

Since intensity goes as the **square** of the surviving amplitude, the secondary maxima fall off roughly as \(1/(2n+1)^{2}\) — the first is about \(1/22\) of the central peak, the second about \(1/61\). The intensity therefore drops sharply, not gently, as the order \(n\) rises.

**The central maximum is also twice as wide as the others**, spanning from \(\theta = -\lambda/a\) to \(+\lambda/a\) while each secondary fringe occupies only \(\lambda/a\). Both facts — twice the width and many times the intensity — come from the same source: only at the centre does the entire slit work together.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: A proton is accelerated through a potential difference V. After acceleration, the de Broglie wavelength associated with it is \(\lambda\). If the proton is replaced by an alpha particle, then find the de Broglie wavelength associated with it if it were accelerated through the same potential difference V. What will be the momentum of the alpha particle ?
rows.solution:
**The wavelength after acceleration through a potential difference.**

A particle of charge \(q\) accelerated from rest through \(V\) gains kinetic energy \(qV\), so its momentum is \(p = \sqrt{2mqV}\) and

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\)

Everything then follows from how \(m\) and \(q\) differ between the two particles. An alpha particle is a helium nucleus:

\(m_\alpha = 4m_p \qquad\text{and}\qquad q_\alpha = 2e = 2q_p\)

**The ratio of the wavelengths.**

Since \(V\) and \(h\) are common to both, they cancel in the ratio:

\(\dfrac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p q_p}{m_\alpha q_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p \cdot q_p}{4m_p \cdot 2q_p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{8}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\)

So

\(\lambda_\alpha = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\lambda \approx 0{\cdot}354\lambda\)

The alpha particle's wave is a little over a third as long as the proton's. Both its greater mass and its greater charge push in the same direction — more mass means more momentum at a given speed, more charge means more energy gained from the same voltage — so neither effect can offset the other.

**The momentum of the alpha particle.**

Momentum and wavelength are reciprocal, \(p = h/\lambda\), so a wavelength \(2\sqrt{2}\) times *shorter* means a momentum \(2\sqrt{2}\) times *larger*:

\(p_\alpha = \dfrac{h}{\lambda_\alpha} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda/2\sqrt{2}}\)

\(p_\alpha = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,h}{\lambda} = 2\sqrt{2}\,p_p \approx 2{\cdot}83\,\dfrac{h}{\lambda}\)

The published scheme prints the intermediate line as \(p_\alpha/p_p = 1/2\sqrt{2}\) before concluding \(p_\alpha = 2\sqrt{2}\,p_p\); the two contradict each other, and it is the **conclusion** that is right. The ratio of momenta is the *inverse* of the ratio of wavelengths, so the line above it has simply carried the \(\lambda\) ratio down unchanged.

A direct check avoids the issue altogether:

\(p_\alpha = \sqrt{2m_\alpha q_\alpha V} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 4m_p \cdot 2q_p \cdot V} = \sqrt{8}\sqrt{2m_p q_p V} = 2\sqrt{2}\,p_p\)

rows.stem: A diver looking up through water \(\left(\mu = \frac{4}{3}\right)\) sees the outside world contained in a circular area on the surface of water. If the diver's eyes are \(\sqrt{7}\) m below the surface of water, then calculate the area of the circle.
rows.solution:
**Why the diver sees a circle at all.**

Light can leave the water only where it meets the surface at less than the **critical angle**; beyond that it is totally internally reflected back down. Running the same path backwards, the diver receives light from the outside world only through a cone of half-angle \(\theta_c\) with its apex at his eye. That cone cuts the flat surface in a **circle**, and everything above the water — the whole hemisphere of sky and shore — is squeezed into it. Outside the circle the diver sees only the mirrored underside of the surface.

**The critical angle.**

\(\sin\theta_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{3}{4}\)

**The radius of the circle.** With the eye at depth \(h\), the radius \(R\) of the circle satisfies

\(\sin\theta_c = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^{2} + h^{2}}}\)

which is the same statement as \(R = h\tan\theta_c\). With \(h = \sqrt{7}\) m:

\(\dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^{2} + 7}}\)

\(16R^{2} = 9(R^{2} + 7) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 7R^{2} = 63\)

\(R = 3\ \mathrm{m}\)

The awkward-looking depth is chosen deliberately: \(\tan\theta_c = 3/\sqrt{7}\), so \(R = \sqrt{7} \times 3/\sqrt{7} = 3\) exactly, and the surd cancels.

**The area.**

\(A = \pi R^{2} = \pi \times 9\)

\(A = 9\pi \approx 28{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)

**Worth noting.** The useful general form is

\(A = \pi h^{2}\tan^{2}\theta_c = \dfrac{\pi h^{2}}{\mu^{2} - 1}\)

so the window grows as the *square* of the depth — a diver twice as deep sees the same sky through a circle four times the area, but no more of the sky itself, since the half-angle \(\theta_c \approx 48{\cdot}6^\circ\) is fixed by the water alone. This is **Snell's window**, and the compression of a full \(180^\circ\) view into \(97^\circ\) is why the world looks distorted and crowded towards its rim when seen from below.
